A decanter and soda siphon on the side table, a cup in hand and two friends in no hurry at all. The older man lounges in a navy double-breasted jacket over grey striped trousers, a dark polka-dot tie at his collar. Across from him sits a grey double-breasted striped suit with a striped tie and white pocket square, legs crossed to reveal grey socks and polished shoes. Both share the double-breasted cut but wear it differently: one as jacket and odd trousers, one as a full suit. Takeaway: a navy double-breasted jacket with striped trousers is an underused alternative to the suit. Would you try it?

Sea breeze, an open fairway and a caddie waiting with the bag. He looks out over the water in a royal blue single-breasted jacket with wide lapels, full-cut grey trousers, a blue shirt and a yellow patterned tie. A white straw hat with a black band and brown and white spectator shoes complete the summer look. The caddie, in a red shirt, white cap and white plus-fours, is no less smart. A blue jacket over grey trousers is a combination that has never gone out of style, and it never will. Would you choose this outfit for a summer weekend?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Two guests descend the stone steps beneath Gothic arches in full morning dress. On the left, a black morning coat with a grey waistcoat, a patterned tie, a red carnation and bold houndstooth trousers, with a slim cane and a silk top hat. On the right, the elder of the pair wears a dark double-breasted overcoat over striped trousers, a white flower in the buttonhole, pale gloves, a cane and his own top hat, his moustache impeccably groomed. It is the kind of occasion where every detail is decided by tradition. Takeaway: formal dress is a uniform that flatters everyone, which is exactly why it endures. Should morning dress make a comeback at weddings?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Off the boat, sun on their faces, heading for lunch. The taller man wears a navy double-breasted blazer with brass buttons, a blue shirt with an open collar, a red pocket square, khaki shorts and a straw hat with a striped band, a towel in hand. His friend wears a red ribbed crewneck sweater and grey pleated shorts. It is the clearest case for the navy blazer: it dresses up shorts as easily as it dresses down flannels. Keep one in your summer rotation and the dock, the club and the restaurant are all covered. Would you wear a blazer with shorts?

Autumn on campus, and the game hasn't started yet. Our man has claimed a bench below the goalposts, pipe in hand, books and a hat resting on his bag, leaves gathering at his feet. The jacket is a bold brown striped cloth with soft shoulders, worn open over a pale shirt and a lively red patterned tie. Brown trousers with deep cuffs break cleanly over dark ribbed socks and fringed kiltie shoes. Nothing matches exactly, and yet everything agrees. The lesson for today: build an outfit around one colour family, then let pattern and texture do the talking. Would you wear the kilties?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Formal daywear, laid out like a lesson.

Top hats, raised in greeting or held at the hip. Cutaway morning coats with their long tails, worn over striped trousers. Shorter black jackets for the men in bowlers and homburg-style hats. Light waistcoats, wing and turndown collars, carnations in the buttonhole, pale gloves, and slim sticks or furled umbrellas at the ready.

Morning dress survives mostly at weddings and race meetings now, yet nothing in menswear signals an occasion quite like it.

Takeaway: if you ever wear a morning coat, keep the trousers striped and the waistcoat light.

Should morning dress make a comeback?

The doorman waits under the striped awning at number 180, and our man steps from his convertible as if he has done it a thousand times. His suit is a soft sage green, double-breasted, with peak lapels and cuffed trousers falling onto brown shoes. A pale fedora with dark band, a green-toned shirt, a striped tie and a gold pocket square keep the palette warm and harmonious. It is proof that colour and tailoring are not enemies. Today's takeaway: if you try a coloured suit, keep the shirt and accessories in the same family so it reads as deliberate. Would you wear a green suit?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Two old friends, two dark pints, and the whole afternoon ahead. Under a striped awning, with a player in whites out on the green beyond, they lounge in wicker chairs. One wears a pale suit with a yellow knit beneath, a straw hat with a blue band, yellow socks and brown slip-ons. The other pairs a deep brown jacket with yellow trousers, a checked tie, a red pocket square and white socks above reddish-brown shoes. Note how both men repeat a single colour, yellow, from top to toe. Borrow that trick: echo one shade in two places and the outfit holds together. Which of the two would you rather sit beside?

He crosses the square as if he owns it, and in that suit perhaps he does. A tall column rises behind him, motorcars wait at the curb, and the soft grey sky only flatters his tailoring. The suit is a grey windowpane check with wide lapels, worn with a pale waistcoat, a spotted bow tie and a white pocket square. A dark hat with a curled brim, white gloves held loosely, a slim crook-handled cane and a neatly clipped moustache finish the picture. The takeaway: windowpane is a pattern that rewards a simple supporting cast, so keep the shirt plain and let the check speak. Spotted bow tie: brave or brilliant?

Every den has its rituals, and this one involves cigars, a football and the morning paper. An older man in spectacles unrolls a large sheet of paper, dressed in a tan single-breasted suit with patch pockets, a plaid tie, a white pocket square and two-tone shoes. Leaning on the panelled wall, a young man wears a navy double-breasted blazer with peak lapels, a navy tie, a white pocket square and cream trousers. A third friend, in grey, turns a football in his hands, and a straw hat rests on a travel trunk. The takeaway: a navy double-breasted blazer with cream trousers is as fresh now as it was then. What would you add to this den?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

'Casa Blanca 37' reads the note beside the signature, and the beach club is in full swing. One man lounges in a folding chair under a wide-brimmed straw hat with a red band, cold glass in hand, wearing a bright plaid short-sleeve shirt, cream trousers, white socks and brown shoes. His friend stands in a red camp-collar shirt and navy high-waisted shorts finished with a wide buckled waistband, plus white shoes trimmed in red. Bathers and umbrellas crowd the shore behind them. The takeaway: high-rise shorts with side adjusters flatter almost everyone and need no belt at all. Which of these two would you rather be this summer?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Between sets, the drinks tray comes out. A soda siphon, tall glasses and the long shadows of a summer afternoon. One player grins in a white short-sleeve shirt, white shorts with a navy side stripe, white socks and navy canvas shoes, a navy jacket slung over his arm. His partner drinks deeply in a white cable-knit cricket sweater trimmed in navy and gold, with full-cut white trousers and white shoes. Tennis whites were a uniform and a courtesy. Keep that spirit: one colour, done properly, always looks intentional. Do you still play in whites?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Ladies and gentlemen of the jury. In a wood-panelled courtroom, a man in a navy double-breasted suit makes his case with open hands. Six buttons, broad peak lapels, a white shirt, a patterned tie and a light pocket square: it is the uniform of quiet authority. The trousers are full and long, falling cleanly to black shoes. Beside him, the accessories of the professional man: a grey hat, a striped shirt with a white collar and cuffs, an array of silk ties, and leather-tabbed braces. Navy double-breasted remains the most persuasive suit a man can own. Would you trust this man with your case?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Two ways to walk into town.

On the left, a dark single-breasted jacket over a matching waistcoat, with grey striped trousers, a bowler, a checked tie, yellow gloves and a slim black stick. A blue flower sits in the lapel. On the right, a navy double-breasted chalk stripe suit with peaked lapels, a red carnation, a white square, a grey snap-brim hat, yellow gloves in hand and a patterned overcoat folded over the arm.

Different moods, same discipline: gloves, a flower, and a hat chosen to match the formality of the suit.

Takeaway: carry your gloves even if you do not wear them.

Bowler and stick, or snap-brim and overcoat?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Books under arm, a spire on the horizon, and a lively debate underway: this is campus life in its best-dressed era. The student on the left wears a brown herringbone single-breasted suit with full trousers, a checked waistcoat, a green knit tie, a dark knit cap and black-and-white spectator shoes. His friend bundles up in a bold herringbone double-breasted overcoat with the collar turned up, worn over checked trousers with white shoes and a brown fedora. Herringbone beside check, and nothing clashes. Takeaway: pattern-mixing works when the scales differ, so pair a bold weave with a quieter check. Which of these two would you wear to class?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Down the steps from the aeroplane, ready for somewhere warm.

Above, a gentleman in round glasses and a pipe wears a navy double-breasted blazer over white trousers, with a white scarf at the neck and a white pocket square. Below him, his fellow passenger has chosen a cream single-breasted suit with patch pockets and turned-up trousers, a striped red-and-green tie, brown shoes and a wide-brimmed tan sun hat.

The takeaway: a navy double-breasted blazer with white trousers, or a cream suit, will see you through almost any warm-weather trip.

Which of these two would you pack?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

The bride stands on the steps, her long train spilling down behind her, and the photographer is ready at his tripod. Around her, the men stand in morning dress: dark tailcoats, waistcoats, boutonnieres and a fine variety of trousers. Most wear the classic stripe, but one guest has chosen a bold check and another a herringbone. The ties range from stripes to small checks. It is a reminder of how much personality fits within a strict dress code. Takeaway: in formal wear, express yourself through the details rather than by breaking the rules. Would you wear morning dress to a wedding today?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

The tackle is ready before the train of thought is. A rod checked by the window, drinks poured, and the river still some way off.

Perched on the edge of a cabinet, our angler wears a grey herringbone suit with full, cuffed trousers, a blue shirt, a dark tie with a white pocket square and striped socks above brown shoes. Beside him lie a plaid coat, a brown hat and a wicker creel. His companion pours in a dark suit with a red flower in his lapel.

Herringbone is the quiet hero of the country wardrobe: textured, forgiving and serious enough for town.

Takeaway: a grey herringbone suit goes almost anywhere.

Where would your herringbone take you?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Paddock side, a moment before the horses are led out. A groom in a flat cap, breeches and tall boots holds a horse in a lettered blanket, while our gentleman looks on, a gloved hand resting on a crook-handled stick. His long overcoat is a bold black and white check, with a badge pinned to the lapel and a strap across his chest. Beneath, a striped tie and checked trousers with cuffs over brown shoes, all topped by a bowler hat. A large-scale check coat is a statement best kept to occasions like this, where tradition invites it. Would you wear this overcoat today?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

White tie is the summit of the dress code, and he carries it lightly.

He leaves the house in a black tailcoat with broad peak lapels, white waistcoat and white bow tie, a red carnation in the buttonhole and a white square at the breast. A top hat and a black overcoat are folded over his arm. Behind him, an older gentleman in the same uniform lights a cigarette while a valet in a striped waistcoat stands ready.

Notice how the waistcoat stays just inside the line of the tailcoat. That clean finish is the mark of correct white tie.

Have you ever attended a white-tie event?

A brisk walk past the shop windows, ties and shirts on display, and two friends dressed for proper cold. On the left, a bold herringbone overcoat, long and generous, worn with a grey hat, striped tie, grey gloves and dark trousers, a slim crook-handled stick at his side. On the right, a soft olive-tan overcoat with flapped patch pockets, paired with a brown hat, a striped tie, tan gloves, checked trousers and brown shoes. Two coats, two moods, both entirely correct. Takeaway: in winter your overcoat is the first thing anyone sees, so choose it with the same care as a suit. Herringbone or plain?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

The car is at the curb, the driver is waiting, and our man pauses for one last word before he leaves.

He wears a long dark single-breasted overcoat that falls well past the knee, a black bowler, pale gloves, and grey striped trousers with turn-ups above polished black shoes. A slim stick completes the city uniform. Beside him on the page: a gingham tie, two striped ties, a detached white collar, and a pair of braces finished with braided gold cords.

The takeaway: a dark overcoat over striped trousers is still the surest way to look ready for anything.

Braces or belt: which do you wear with tailored trousers?

Game day in the stadium, and the cold has not dampened anyone's spirits. Our man wears a double-breasted overcoat in grey with a blue windowpane check, a navy scarf with white spots at the neck, and a dark hat with a feather in the band. Yellow gloves, a blanket over his arm and a leather case on a strap show a man who came prepared. To the side, the accessories of the day: a plaid stadium rug with fringed ends, a green felt hat with a feather, a buckled overshoe, and two patterned handkerchiefs. The lesson: dress for the weather, but never forget to dress. What do you bring to a cold-weather game?

10 AM, Boston Express. The board says so, the porter is already lifting bags, and our traveller has all the time in the world. His overcoat is the star: a long double-breasted herringbone in bold grey, with broad peak lapels, flap pockets and a full skirt that falls well below the knee. Beneath it, navy striped trousers with turn-ups and black shoes. A dark felt hat, a striped tie, light gloves and a slim walking stick finish the picture, while a suitcase with a French flag sticker hints at where he has been. A good overcoat is the one garment everyone sees first. Is a long double-breasted coat still worth the investment?

Gabardine jacket, flannel slacks and fashionable accessories. So reads the handwritten note beside this figure, and it remains one of the most reliable formulas in a man's wardrobe. The jacket is a warm tan single-breasted model with a white pocket square; the trousers are grey flannel, pleated, full through the leg and finished with deep turn-ups. A red patterned tie, a white hat with a dark band and brown-and-white spectator shoes supply the accessories in question. Odd jacket, grey trousers: master this pairing and half your wardrobe follows. What would you swap in for the spectators today?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Not every lesson in style needs a tie. Beneath a beach awning, a sun-browned man rests on a wicker settee in a navy-and-white striped short-sleeved top, the sailor's stripe carried ashore. His grey shorts have a blue stripe down the side and a matching blue belt, and on his feet are white canvas shoes laced up around the ankle. Behind him, bathers stroll past in robes and swimsuits. The takeaway still holds: keep resort clothes to two or three colours, and let a single classic pattern do the work. Is the striped top the most enduring summer garment ever made?

Somewhere above the clouds, in deep wingback seats with footstools to spare, the cabin settles into a comfortable hush. One passenger dozes; another reads a magazine with complete composure. Both wear bold check suits, the kind of glen check and plaid patterns that come alive in natural light. The reader adds a striped tie, a white pocket square and a red flower in his lapel, a small gesture that changes the whole outfit. A stewardess keeps watch from the aisle. The lesson for modern travel: a soft, patterned suit can be just as comfortable as any tracksuit, and far better company. Would you board a flight dressed like this?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

"Many of the old rules are off," the caption declares, "particularly the one that said the jacket had to be darker than the slacks."

The illustration proves the point. Perched on a poolside railing, our man wears a bold black-and-white houndstooth sport jacket over rust-brown trousers, full in the leg with deep turn-ups. A light hat, a yellow shirt and brown-and-white spectator shoes keep the mood sunny, while swimmers lounge below. Belts, ties and a shirt float in the margin, a whole wardrobe on one page.

The lesson still holds: a lighter, louder jacket over darker trousers looks relaxed and deliberate.

Do you follow the old rule or break it?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Pipe lit, weight on his stick, he looks ready for a long country walk and a longer conversation. This is rural dressing at its most cheerful: a soft cap, a spotted yellow neckerchief at the throat, and a canary-yellow single-breasted waistcoat under a textured olive jacket with flap pockets. Matching trousers with turn-ups run down to brown shoes, and a small red pocket square adds a spark. The palette is rustic, but the fit is unmistakably tailored, from the easy shoulder to the clean trouser line. Takeaway: a bright odd waistcoat is the simplest way to bring personality to country clothes. Would you dare the yellow waistcoat?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Striped cabanas, palm fronds and three ways to dress for the same beach. One man rests on the step in a white jacket and navy shorts. The middle fellow wears a printed short-sleeve shirt, olive pleated trousers, white shoes and a wide straw hat. On the right, a brown double-breasted suit with peak lapels, a patterned tie, a white pocket square and two-tone spectator shoes, with a straw hat in a patterned band raised in greeting. Same heat, three different levels of formality, all of them correct. The lesson: dress for where the day might take you, not just the sand. Which of the three is your style?

By the pool, the dress code is whatever you can carry off. The standing young man keeps it simple: a red and white striped knit shirt with a navy collar, red shorts, a white belt and woven sandals. His seated friend goes all in. A double-breasted suit in an orange and cream plaid with peak lapels, a red silk scarf patterned in yellow at the throat, a white pocket square, striped socks and white shoes. It should not work, and yet it does, because the warm colours repeat from head to toe. Bold patterns need a common thread. Could you pull off the plaid suit?

Somewhere warm, under the palms, the afternoon has gone pleasantly idle. In an open carriage, one passenger dozes in a cream jacket and green tie, a young woman in red smiles beside him, and a companion in a bowler and bow tie strums a small stringed instrument. The young man perched on the side is the style lesson: a crisp white shirt with a chest pocket, a navy striped tie, a belt, light grey trousers, blue socks and a grey hat with a dark band. Cyclists pass along the waterfront behind. Take note: a white shirt, a good tie and pale trousers make a complete summer outfit, jacket optional. Would you go jacketless with a tie?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

The party has spilled onto the steps, and the champagne has followed. While the crowd carries on above, one man in a tan peak-lapel dinner jacket fills a glass for his companion in a striped gown. A black bow tie, white shirt, white pocket square and black trousers complete his black tie. Behind him the room is a catalogue of evening options: a grey double-breasted dinner jacket, a white dinner jacket, and the classic black. Black tie has always allowed more variety than people assume. The rule is simple: keep the trousers dark and the bow tie black. Which jacket colour would you choose?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

Two friends, two very different answers to the same summer afternoon. On the left, a pale grey suit with a bold red pinstripe, single-breasted with wide lapels, worn with a spotted bow tie, a red flower in the buttonhole, a white pocket square and a light hat carried in hand. On the right, a navy double-breasted suit with peak lapels, a spotted navy tie, a striped shirt with a white collar, a blue flower at the lapel and a straw boater. Both finish with tan shoes and full trousers with turn-ups. The lesson: brown shoes with navy or grey is not a rule broken but a summer tradition. Left or right?

The lettering beside the signature reads 'Casa Blanca', and the scene has all the ease of a sunlit terrace under striped awnings. One man leans, hand on hip, in a red plaid short-sleeve shirt, high-waisted pleated shorts and red espadrille-style shoes. His older companion, pipe clenched, keeps a touch of formality: a tan jacket with a white pocket square, a red neckerchief, grey shorts, white socks and blue shoes. It is a masterclass in warm-weather dressing without a hint of sloppiness. The takeaway: shorts can be tailored, pleated and worn at the natural waist, and they look far better for it. Would you wear a jacket with shorts?

Illustration: Laurence Fellows

A guidebook marked 1939 tells you where we are: the fairgrounds, the future on display, and two visitors determined to see all of it.

The man on the left, camera hanging at his chest, wears a light grey chalk stripe suit with a yellow tie, a pocket square and a brown fedora. His companion has gone bolder: a double-breasted glen plaid suit with a red overcheck, a tan fedora, a striped tie and a pipe in hand.

Both suits are cut full in the trouser with turn-ups, the way a man dressed for a long day on his feet.

Takeaway: a light suit and a soft hat suit a summer day out.

Stripe or plaid for sightseeing?

The car is at the kerb, the chauffeur waits at the wheel and the luggage is already being carried off. Our traveller pauses on the pavement mid-story, briefcase in hand. His camel-coloured double-breasted overcoat has broad peak lapels and falls well below the knee, worn over grey striped trousers with turn-ups. A striped shirt, a dark polka-dot tie, tan gloves and a green fedora finish it. Notice how nothing clashes: earth tones on the outside, quiet patterns at the neck. A good camel coat is still the best travelling companion a man can own. Where would you be off to in this coat?

Sun on the boardwalk, swimmers in the pool and a pipe going slowly. The gentleman at the rail has nailed resort tailoring: a grey double-breasted jacket with peak lapels, cream pleated trousers with turn-ups and a navy polka-dot scarf tucked into an open collar, under a dark snap-brim hat. Even his shoes are a bit of fun, in a spotted print. Behind him, an older man strolls in a striped short-sleeve shirt, navy trousers and white shoes. The point is simple: tailoring by the water works when the jacket is crisp and the trousers are light. Would you swap the tie for a scarf on a summer afternoon?

Race day at the rail, and the gentlemen are as well turned out as the horses. On the left, a young man in a dark navy jacket with peak lapels, a boater and a polka-dot bow tie, a leather binocular case at his hip. Beside him, an older man with a white moustache wears a bold grey plaid suit over a buff waistcoat, with a dark hat, striped tie, crook-handled cane and his own binocular case on a strap. Race cards in hand, they talk form. The lesson: sporting events invite bolder patterns, so wear them with confidence. Boater or dark hat for a day at the races?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows

A light for the cigarette, a smile from the lady in yellow and a whole group dressed for a warm afternoon. On the left, a grey double-breasted suit and a straw hat with a dark band. Beside him, a tan suit with a red bow tie. In the centre, a glen check jacket over brown trousers, and at the back a cream jacket with a red patterned pocket square over grey trousers, a straw hat in hand. Five people, five colours, all in harmony. The lesson: a group looks best when each man dresses well rather than identically. Which of these jackets would you choose?
Illustration: Laurence Fellows
